mcq.prompt: Why is `std::strlen` an O(n) operation while `std::string::size()` is O(1)?
choices: strlen validates the encoding as it scans
std::string caches the length only after the first call to size()
A C string encodes its length as a terminating '\0', so the length can only be found by scanning to it
strlen must handle unaligned buffers and therefore proceeds one byte at a time
mcq.explain: The terminator *is* the length encoding: nothing in a `const char*` records how many characters there are, so every length query walks the buffer until it reaches the zero byte. std::string and std::string_view both store the count as a member, so size() is a load. Alignment and encoding have nothing to do with it — a vectorised strlen is still O(n).

mcq.prompt: `char raw[3]{'F', 'I', 'X'};` is passed to `std::strlen`. What happens?
choices: Undefined behaviour: strlen reads past the end of the array searching for a zero
It returns 3, because the array's bound is known at the call site
It returns 0, because the array was not zero-initialised
The call is ill-formed, because char[3] does not convert to const char*
mcq.explain: The array holds three characters and no terminator, and the parameter decayed to a bare `const char*` that carries no bound, so strlen keeps reading past the end until it happens to find a zero byte. The array's size was known to the compiler at the call site but is not part of what the function receives — that lost size is exactly what made strcpy and its relatives a recurring source of buffer overflows.

mcq.prompt: Which guarantee does `std::string` provide that `std::vector<char>` does not?
choices: Contiguous storage of its elements
Geometric growth on append
An unchecked operator[] alongside a checked at()
A null terminator readable at data()[size()]
mcq.explain: Since C++11 a string guarantees a readable '\0' one past the last character, which is what makes c_str() a constant-time operation rather than a copy. Contiguity, geometric growth, and the operator[]/at() pair are the vector model that string simply inherits — the terminator and the text-specific API (find, substr, starts_with) are the additions.

mcq.prompt: A `const char* saved = message.data();` is taken, then `message += suffix;` reallocates. What is the status of `saved`?
choices: Still valid — data() returns a pointer that the string keeps updated
Dangling, exactly as a pointer into a std::vector is after the vector grows
Still valid, but only for reading the first size() characters
Still valid, because the terminator guarantee forces the string to keep the old buffer alive
mcq.explain: A string is the vector model applied to characters, so a reallocation moves the characters to new storage and frees the old buffer; every saved pointer, reference and iterator into it dangles. Nothing about data() creates a subscription to future changes, and the terminator guarantee is about the new buffer's layout, not about keeping the old one alive.

mcq.prompt: What does the small-string optimization actually buy, and what does it cost?
choices: It shrinks sizeof(std::string); it costs an extra indirection on every access
It makes short strings immutable; it costs a copy on first write
It stores short strings inside the string object, avoiding a heap allocation; it costs a mode branch in common operations
It guarantees strings under 15 bytes never reallocate; it costs a fixed 15-byte overhead per string
mcq.explain: SSO holds the characters inside the string object itself, so a short value never reaches the allocator. The object must then be able to tell inline mode from heap mode, which puts a usually-predictable branch inside data(), size() and append(). It makes the object *larger*, not smaller, and the inline capacity is a library ABI detail — roughly 15 bytes in libstdc++, 22 in libc++, and neither number is portable.

mcq.prompt: A pointer is taken into a short `std::string`, and the string is then moved into another object. What is true of that pointer?
choices: It is dangling or points into the moved-from object, because moving an SSO string copies the inline characters
It follows the characters into the destination, because a move transfers ownership of the buffer
It stays valid because a moved-from string is guaranteed to retain its value
It stays valid only if the destination was default-constructed
mcq.explain: Moving a heap-backed string can steal the pointer in constant time, but an SSO string has no pointer to steal: its characters must be copied into the destination's own inline buffer. The saved pointer still refers to storage inside the source object, whose value after the move is valid but unspecified. A string move is cheap; it is not a promise that pointers into the source survive.

mcq.prompt: How should a `std::string_view` parameter be declared?
choices: const std::string_view&, to avoid copying the view
std::string_view by value — it is a pointer and a length, so copying it is trivial
std::string_view&&, so a view over a temporary can be moved
const std::string_view*, so an absent argument can be expressed
mcq.explain: A view is normally two machine words with no ownership, so passing it by value costs the same as passing two integers and keeps it in registers. Taking it by const reference adds an indirection to every access and buys nothing, since there is no allocation or copy to avoid; there is likewise nothing to move, because the view does not own the characters.

mcq.prompt: `void log(const std::string& text)` is called as `log("a fairly long literal message")`. What happens that `void log(std::string_view text)` would avoid?
choices: The literal is copied into read-only memory before the call
The literal's terminator is scanned twice, once by strlen and once by the constructor
The call is ambiguous and requires an explicit conversion
A temporary std::string is constructed, which for input this long allocates and copies the characters
mcq.explain: `const std::string&` still requires a std::string to bind to, so the literal is used to construct a temporary one — beyond the inline SSO capacity that means a heap allocation and a character copy per call. A string_view represents the literal directly as a pointer and a length, which is also why one such parameter accepts literals, owning strings, and slices alike.

mcq.prompt: A `std::string_view symbol` is formed over the middle of a larger buffer, and `symbol.data()` is handed to a C function taking `const char*`. What is wrong?
choices: The C function reads from data() until it finds a '\0', which is not where the view ends — undefined behaviour, or at best the wrong text
Nothing, because string_view always keeps a terminator one past its last character
data() returns const char*, so the call will not compile
The C function receives the whole underlying buffer, which is inefficient but correct
mcq.explain: A view is a pointer and a length; the length is the only thing that marks its end, and nothing guarantees a zero byte there. If the buffer has no zero at all the C function reads out of bounds, and if one exists further along it silently receives more text than the view described. The fix is an explicit bridge — construct `std::string terminated{symbol}` and pass terminated.c_str() — which owns and terminates the characters, at the cost of a possible allocation.

mcq.prompt: Where does the `std::string terminated{view}; some_c_api(terminated.c_str());` bridge belong?
choices: Anywhere — the conversion is free because string_view already stores the characters
Inside the view-producing function, so callers never see the unterminated form
Outside the hot path, because constructing the std::string copies the characters and can allocate
It should never be used; reinterpreting the view's data() is always preferable
mcq.explain: The bridge is correct and sometimes unavoidable, but it is the one place in a view-based parser that owns and copies characters, and beyond the inline capacity it allocates. Keep it at the boundary where the C API is actually called rather than repeating it per field on a hot path. A view stores no characters of its own, so there is no cheaper conversion to reach for.

mcq.prompt: `std::string_view view = name + "_US";` where `name` is a live `std::string`. When does the view become invalid?
choices: When `name` is next modified
Immediately: the temporary holding the concatenation is destroyed at the end of that full expression
When `name` goes out of scope, since the view refers into it
Never — binding to a view extends the temporary's lifetime, as binding to a const reference does
mcq.explain: `name + "_US"` produces a temporary std::string that dies at the semicolon, and the view — which merely recorded that temporary's pointer and length — is dangling before the next statement runs. Lifetime extension applies to binding a temporary to a const reference; a string_view is an ordinary object that copies a pointer, so it extends nothing. The view never refers into `name` at all; the concatenation built fresh storage.

mcq.prompt: A `std::string_view` is bound to a `std::string owner` that stays in scope for the whole function. Under what circumstance can the view still dangle?
choices: It cannot — the owner outliving every use is exactly the required condition
Only if the owner is const, because a const string may be placed in read-only storage
Only if the owner is moved from
If the owner is mutated in a way that reallocates, or moved from, its old character buffer dies while the object lives on
mcq.explain: View validity is pointer validity, not object validity. An append that outgrows the current capacity frees the old buffer, so the still-living owner now holds different storage than the view points at; a move can relocate the characters for the same reason. The review rule is to treat every view into an owner as invalid after any mutation of that owner, rather than reasoning about which operations happen to reallocate.

mcq.prompt: A class is constructed from a by-value `std::string symbol` parameter and needs to keep the text. What should the member be?
choices: A std::string, moved from the parameter — the parameter dies at the end of the constructor
A std::string_view over the parameter, since the caller supplied the storage
A const char*, taken from symbol.c_str()
A std::string_view, provided the constructor is documented as requiring a long-lived argument
mcq.explain: The by-value parameter is a local object that is destroyed when the constructor returns, so both a view over it and a pointer into it dangle immediately — the caller's storage is not what the parameter refers to. Move the parameter into an owning std::string member. A view member is only defensible when an explicit contract names who owns the characters and how long they stay stable, and a by-value parameter is the opposite of that.

mcq.prompt: What is the difference between `std::span<int>` and `std::span<const int>`?
choices: span<const int> stores its length as a constant known at compile time
span<const int> owns a copy of the elements; span<int> refers to the originals
span<int> permits mutation of the referred-to elements; span<const int> does not
span<const int> can only be constructed from a const container
mcq.explain: The element type controls writability: span<T> hands out mutable references, span<const T> read-only ones, which is the span analogue of string_view's read-only role. Neither owns anything — both are a pointer and a length over storage someone else holds. A compile-time length comes from a fixed extent, span<T, N>, which is an independent choice.

mcq.prompt: What does the fixed extent in `std::span<const std::byte, 8>` change compared with `std::span<const std::byte>`?
choices: It bounds-checks operator[] at runtime and throws std::out_of_range
The size lives in the type, so the object need only store a pointer and a mismatched array is rejected at compile time
It makes the span own eight bytes of inline storage
It makes the span convertible to a std::array<const std::byte, 8>
mcq.explain: A fixed extent moves the length from a runtime member into the type: implementations need store only the pointer, construction from an array of the wrong size fails to compile, and the bound is available to the optimiser. It adds no runtime checking — the pointer-and-count constructor requires the count to equal the extent, and violating that precondition is undefined behaviour in C++23. The span still owns nothing.

mcq.prompt: A function returns a `std::span<int>` over a `std::vector<int>` member, and the caller then pushes onto that vector. What is the status of the span?
choices: Valid — a span tracks its source container
Valid, because the vector's element type did not change
Valid until the vector is destroyed, and no earlier
Potentially dangling, because a push_back that reallocates frees the storage the span points at
mcq.explain: A span is subject to exactly the lifetime discipline of a string_view: it stores a pointer and a length, so it dangles when its source dies *and* when the source reallocates. A push_back that exceeds capacity moves the elements to new storage and frees the old, leaving the span pointing at freed memory; the stored length is now wrong as well. Nothing in the span observes the container.

mcq.prompt: A 2×3 grid is viewed through `std::mdspan` with `std::layout_right`. Which index should vary in the innermost loop for the best traversal locality?
choices: The rightmost index, because layout_right makes it the contiguous one
The leftmost index, because layout_right places the leftmost extent first in memory
Either — mdspan copies the elements into its own layout
Neither; mdspan traversal order is chosen by the implementation
mcq.explain: layout_right makes the rightmost index contiguous, matching row-major C-style storage, so stepping that index walks adjacent elements. layout_left is the mirror image and matches column-major Fortran and BLAS conventions. mdspan owns and moves nothing — the same flat buffer can be viewed under either policy, and only the index-to-offset mapping changes.

mcq.section: from_chars and to_chars: number conversion for hot paths
mcq.prompt: A parser calls `from_chars` and accepts the field whenever `error == std::errc{}`. What input slips through?
choices: An empty field, which from_chars reports as success
A field with leading whitespace, which from_chars silently skips
A field with a valid numeric prefix and trailing junk, such as "100.25oops"
A field whose value overflows the target type, which from_chars reports only through errno
mcq.explain: from_chars consumes the longest valid prefix and reports success for it, so "100.25oops" parses as 100.25 with no error — the returned pointer is what says the field was not fully consumed. Comparing `next == end` is the check that enforces full-field consumption. The other cases are already handled: an empty or non-numeric field gives invalid_argument, an out-of-range value gives result_out_of_range, and from_chars deliberately does not skip leading whitespace.

mcq.section: from_chars and to_chars: number conversion for hot paths
mcq.prompt: Which set of properties distinguishes `std::from_chars` from `std::stod` for a hot parsing path?
choices: It is constexpr, throws on error, and requires a null-terminated input
It is locale-free, non-allocating and non-throwing, reporting errors through an errc and an end pointer
It is faster only because it skips validation entirely
It supports more numeric formats, including hexadecimal and thousands separators
mcq.explain: from_chars touches no locale, no heap and no exception machinery: it scans the supplied range and returns an std::errc plus a pointer to the first unconsumed character. std::stod is locale-dependent, often allocates when given a view, and signals failure by throwing. from_chars validates more strictly than the alternatives, not less — it refuses even leading whitespace — and it takes a range rather than requiring a terminator, which is why string_view::data() plus size() is exactly the right input.

mcq.prompt: How do `std::string::substr` and `std::string_view::substr` differ in cost?
choices: Both are constant time; string::substr shares the original buffer with reference counting
string::substr is constant time; string_view::substr is linear because it must find the end
They are identical — string::substr returns a view in C++20 and later
string::substr allocates and copies the characters into a new owning string; string_view::substr only adjusts a pointer and a length
mcq.explain: string::substr returns a new owning std::string, so it copies the selected characters and allocates whenever they exceed the inline capacity. string_view::substr is pointer arithmetic over storage that already exists and returns another view in constant time — as do remove_prefix and remove_suffix, which narrow the window in place. Copy-on-write reference counting for std::string has been forbidden since C++11.

reading.explain: sizeof reports the array's storage — sixteen bytes, whatever is in them — while strlen answers the unrelated question of how many characters precede the first zero, which it must scan for. The tempting reading is that writing a zero at index 4 destroyed the rest of the line; it did not. The bytes are untouched, only the C string's end moved: strlen(header) becomes 4, and strlen(header + 6) still finds "quant.io" and reports 8. Copy-initialising a char[16] from a 14-character literal zero-fills the remaining bytes, so header[15] is 0. Length is encoded, not stored, which is why a C string can be shortened by a single store and why nothing a `const char*` receives can tell you the buffer now holds two of them.

remove_prefix narrows the view it is called on, and that view is a by-value parameter — a private copy of the caller's pointer and length. The function reports true, but main's window is as wide as before: 23 characters still beginning with "https". The tempting answer, `true 15 quant`, assumes remove_prefix either edits characters or reaches back through the parameter; it does neither, since a view owns nothing and narrowing it is arithmetic on its own two members. Passing a view by value is right precisely because it is two words, but a router written this way has to return the narrowed view, or take `std::string_view&`, for the caller to see it.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: std::string's constructor from a string-view-like type is explicit, so `return word;` — a copy-initialisation of the return object — finds no viable conversion and the translation unit is rejected. The tempting reading is that because a std::string converts implicitly *to* a string_view, the reverse must work too; the asymmetry is deliberate. Owner to view costs nothing and cannot allocate, while view to owner copies the characters and may call the allocator, so the standard makes that direction something you write down: `return std::string{word};`.

reading.prompt: What happens when this is compiled and run?
reading.explain: A span is a pointer and a length over storage it does not own, so it follows exactly the discipline a string_view does: it dangles when its source dies *and* when its source moves the elements. The vector was built from a four-element initialiser list, so its capacity is four and the push_back must reallocate — the elements go to fresh storage and the old block is freed, leaving `window` pointing into it. The read-modify-write is then a heap-use-after-free, which ASan reports. The tempting reading is that `samples` is still alive and still holds five doubles, so the window must still name one of them; object lifetime is not the question, pointer validity is. Nothing in a span observes its container, and the stored length of 2 is stale as well.

reading.section: from_chars and to_chars: number conversion for hot paths
reading.explain: from_chars does not skip leading whitespace, so the space before the 7 is not a harmless formatting detail: it is the first character of the range and it is not a digit. The call fails with invalid_argument, leaves `retries` at its previous -1 rather than zeroing it, and returns a pointer equal to its first argument, so the offset prints as 0. The tempting answer, `0 7 2`, is what std::atoi or std::strtod would have trained you to expect, since those do skip whitespace and would silently accept the field. Note what did work: `config` contains no terminator anywhere, and neither substr nor from_chars needed one, because a view's data() and size() describe the range exactly.

reserve sets capacity, not size, so the string is still empty afterwards and `base` names the start of a buffer holding no characters. Every append then lands inside that reservation: a string reallocates only when its size would exceed its capacity, and capacity never shrinks on its own, so the buffer is never replaced and data() still equals `base` — the appends are pure stores, and any pointer or view taken after the reserve would have survived them. The tempting reading is that reserve pre-sized the string, making the result 64 characters long or leaving fourteen bytes of filler in front of the appended text. The last check is deliberately an inequality: an implementation may reserve more than asked, so an exact capacity is never a portable thing to assert.

writing.prompt: A C logging API takes `const char*`. Write `bool to_c_string(std::string_view text, std::span<char> buffer)` that copies `text` into the caller-supplied buffer and null-terminates it. It must allocate nothing, must not assume `text` is followed by a zero byte, must reserve room for the terminator, and must return false rather than truncate when the text does not fit.
checklist: Allocates nothing: no std::string, no new — the caller owns the storage
Rejects the call when buffer.size() < text.size() + 1, so the terminator is accounted for
Copies exactly text.size() characters, driven by size() rather than by any C string function applied to the view
Writes '\0' at buffer[text.size()] on success
Takes std::string_view and std::span<char> by value
writing.notes: This is the allocation-free form of the `std::string terminated{view}; api(terminated.c_str());` bridge: the characters still have to be copied and terminated somewhere, but here the caller decides where, so a hot path can reuse one stack buffer instead of visiting the allocator per call. std::strncpy is not a substitute — it terminates only when the source is shorter than the count, and it would treat the view as a C string in the first place. The empty guard is not decoration either: passing a null data() to memcpy is undefined even for a zero count.

writing.prompt: An INI parser needs `std::string_view trim(std::string_view text)` that strips leading and trailing spaces and tabs. It must allocate nothing and copy no characters, must return an empty view when the input is entirely blank or empty, and its result must still point into the caller's original storage.
checklist: Returns std::string_view and performs no allocation and no character copy
Strips both spaces and tabs, from both ends
Handles an all-blank or empty input by returning an empty view rather than computing a length from npos
Narrows the window with remove_prefix/remove_suffix or substr instead of building a new string
Never requires the input to be null-terminated
writing.notes: The all-blank case is the one that bites: find_last_not_of returns npos there, and `npos + 1` is 0, so trimming the suffix first and the prefix afterwards silently produces a nonsense length. One check of find_first_not_of up front settles it. Everything else is arithmetic on a pointer and a length, so a whole config file can be tokenised without a single allocation — and every returned view is only as valid as the buffer the caller passed in.

writing.section: from_chars and to_chars: number conversion for hot paths
writing.prompt: Timeouts arrive as text such as `"150ms"` or `"30s"`. Write `parse_duration(std::string_view text)` returning a `struct Duration { bool ok; std::int64_t count; std::string_view unit; }`, where `unit` is the unparsed remainder *as a view into the input*. Use `std::from_chars`. It must not allocate, must not throw, must not require the input to be null-terminated, and must report failure when no digits could be consumed or the value is out of range.
checklist: Calls std::from_chars over text.data() and text.data() + text.size()
Reports failure for both invalid_argument and result_out_of_range
Derives the suffix from the pointer from_chars returned, not from a second scan for the first non-digit
Returns the suffix as a std::string_view into the caller's text, with no allocation
A bare number with no suffix succeeds and yields an empty unit
Includes <charconv>
writing.notes: Here the returned pointer is the product rather than merely an error check: from_chars stops at the first character it could not consume, which is exactly where the unit begins, so no second scan is needed. It is also why `next == end` is only sometimes the right test — a full-field parser must reject a remainder, a suffixed-value parser has to consume it. Since from_chars refuses leading whitespace, `" 150ms"` fails outright instead of parsing quietly, and the unit view costs nothing because it points into the caller's characters.

writing.prompt: This log sink caches a view of the most recently written line. Explain in a comment why `last()` is unsafe, then fix the class so that `last()` is valid until the next call to `write`. Keep the accessor returning `std::string_view` and keep every line in the single `text_` buffer — do not add a second owning string member.
checklist: Comment names both hazards: last_ aliases the caller's argument, whose lifetime the Journal does not control, and any view into text_ dies when an append reallocates
The view member is replaced by an offset and a length into text_
last() rebuilds the view from text_ at the point of the call
write still appends the line and a newline to text_, with no extra owning copy of the line
The offset is captured before the append, so it names the start of the new line
writing.notes: Indices are the standard answer whenever a stored reference into a growable container would have to survive a mutation — the same reasoning that rules out keeping pointers into a std::vector across push_back. The view last() hands out is still governed by the usual rule: it is valid until the next write, and the class should document that, because the caller cannot see the append that will invalidate it.

writing.prompt: Write two functions for a sample-processing pipeline: `scale(samples, factor)`, which multiplies every sample in place, and `newest(samples, count)`, which returns a read-only window on the last `count` samples and must clamp when fewer than `count` exist. Neither may copy the samples, and both must accept a `double[]`, a `std::array<double, N>` and a `std::vector<double>` with no overloading and no templates of your own.
checklist: scale takes std::span<double> (mutable elements); newest takes std::span<const double>
Both spans are taken by value, and neither function is a template or names a container type
scale mutates through the span rather than copying elements out and back
newest clamps count to samples.size() instead of handing an oversized count to last
newest returns std::span<const double> built with last or subspan — no new container
writing.notes: The element type carries the permission: span<double> hands out mutable references and therefore cannot be constructed from a const container at all, while span<const double> accepts either and forbids writing. One non-template parameter absorbing arrays, std::array and vector alike is the span analogue of a single string_view parameter absorbing literals, strings and slices. Both the passed and the returned span point into the caller's storage and are only as valid as it is.

writing.prompt: Write `join(std::span<const std::string_view> parts, char separator)` returning a `std::string` — one CSV row built from its fields. Compute the exact final length and reserve it once before appending anything, so that no growth occurs during the build. There must be no separator after the last field, an empty input must produce an empty string, and empty fields in the middle must be preserved.
checklist: Computes the total length, separators included, before the first append
Calls reserve exactly once, before any append
Builds with append or operator+= only — no operator+ chain and no intermediate std::string
Emits separators between fields only, leaving no trailing one
Returns an empty string for an empty span without underflowing the separator count
writing.notes: An `a + b + c` chain would instead create a temporary string per addition, each free to acquire its own capacity and each copying everything accumulated so far. Reserving the measured total turns the whole row into one allocation followed by pure stores. The empty guard earns its place: parts.size() - 1 is unsigned arithmetic, so on an empty span it wraps to an enormous reserve request. Reserve changes capacity only, so the string is still empty when the appends begin.
